Discussion for #Project announcements > Ship Your Interpreters @ 💬

https://github.com/BasisResearch/ship-your-interpreter/
Formal Semantics are a necessary precursor to enable program verification. Unfortunately most programming languages do not have any semantics.
One might be tempted to use LLMs to generate these semantics, but as semantics form part of your trusted spec, and semantics for real world languages tend to be very complex, these artefacts are large and hard to trust.
Can we get LLMs to build program semantics that can be trusted?

Answer? Yes! Ship your interpreter! That is you can compile your programming language interpreter to RISCV (which has a formal model in Lean), and then validate the LLM generated semantics by proving that the interpreter refines the big step semantics

Isn't one of the insights from formalizing semantics of real world languages that the interpreter is usually broken or semantically undesirable in some shape or form? Which is to say, isn't it quite likely that we end up generating an undesirable semantics with this approach?

I guess this really depends on the eye of the beholder. For end-users, what they care about when a program is proven, is that whatever property is stated, holds on the "real code" that runs in prod.

The real code that runs in prod probably doesn't match the platonic ideal of what the language "should do".

I could prove some beautiful property about my program w.r.t Python's /moral semantics/, but it means jack if in practice the CPython interpreter does something completely different.

Given that most interest in verification is coming from the perspective of securing real world code (often using fixed toolchains and language versions), this meets users closer to where they are at.

And sure, then we discover ugly points in the generated semantics we can go back to the language authors and ask them to fix their PLs, but this is a second order process in comparison to verifying the real code that is deployed in practice.

(One other thing that has stood out to me in talking with Kiran about this is that some _subset_ of the language may have a more well-behaved semantics, which may also be good enough. I think it's an open question how much of Python lies in the easy-to-model fragment but I think it's more than none.)

Have you tried ship-your-interpreter on languages that are intermediate between "WHILE -lang" and "Python"? I'd be curious what transfers as you go towards larger / more "production" languages. I'm thinking good candidates are dc/bc (which has some programs in the wild), scheme, or esolangs (some of which have human-written Lean semantics)

Not yet! I think tackling Python in full is something that might need a bit more compute than I have access to at the moment ;). A language inbetween which I think might be fun to try is Lua!

Honestly, the proof just went through on Friday, I wasn't expecting it to go through so quickly - it had been stalling for a few weeks, and I asked an agent to port it to Iris-Lean and on the same day all the remaining obligations pretty much were done with the port.

My focus since then has been on playing around with some of the things you can build ontop of a verified end-to-end semantics as proof of concept, but now I am confident it's feasible with current models, I am very eager to try on a bigger language next.

Given how often Lua is embedded as a scripting language (for example into the NeoVim editor that many users here apparently use (I'm an Emacs user for reference)), I think it'd be quite practical to have a verified Lua semantics!

Kiran said:

I think tackling Python in full is something that might need a bit more compute than I have access to at the moment

Do you think there is a reasonable way to break this big problem down into smaller milestones that could be accomplished with only a handful of LLM subscriptions? i.e. Markus above mentions that there may be some well-behaved subset of python which is easier to model and may still cover a large subset of real python program behavior.

Kiran said:

Honestly, the proof just went through on Friday, I wasn't expecting it to go through so quickly - it had been stalling for a few weeks, and I asked an agent to port it to Iris-Lean and on the same day all the remaining obligations pretty much were done with the port.

Can you explain a bit on what "porting to Iris-Lean" did for this project? In particular, I'd be curious to know what features of Iris your agents leveraged that they weren't able to come up with from scratch when trying to close the proofs.
